questions.stem: The meeting was called ______ due to bad weather.
questions.explanation: A is correct. CALL OFF = to cancel an event or activity. 'The meeting was called off' = the meeting was cancelled. Other 'call' phrasal verbs: call up (phone/summon), call on (visit/invite to speak), call out (challenge), call for (demand), call in (request someone's presence).

questions.stem: She found it very difficult to put ______ with her noisy neighbours.
questions.explanation: A is correct. PUT UP WITH = to tolerate or endure something unpleasant. Important 'put' phrasal verbs: put up (accommodate/tolerate), put off (postpone/discourage), put out (extinguish), put down (criticise/record), put across (communicate clearly), put forward (suggest), put through (connect a call/make endure).

questions.stem: He eventually gave ______ to the pressure and resigned.
questions.explanation: C is correct. GIVE IN TO = to yield or surrender (often to pressure, demands, or temptation). Note the preposition 'to' follows: 'gave in to the pressure'. Give up = quit something; give in = submit to external force. Other 'give' phrasal verbs: give away (donate/reveal), give out (distribute), give back (return), give over (transfer).

questions.stem: The teacher asked the students to look ______ the new words in the dictionary.
questions.explanation: B is correct. LOOK UP = to search for a word/information in a reference (dictionary, directory). 'Look up the new words' = find their meanings in the dictionary. 'Look' phrasal verbs: look after (care for), look up (search in reference), look into (investigate), look out (be careful), look forward to (anticipate), look over (review), look down on (feel superior to).

questions.stem: The company decided to take ______ more staff for the holiday season.
questions.explanation: A is correct. TAKE ON = (1) to hire/employ someone; (2) to undertake a task; (3) to confront a challenge. 'Take on more staff' = hire more employees. 'Take' phrasal verbs: take on (hire/undertake), take off (remove/depart/become popular), take over (assume control), take up (start activity/occupy space), take back (retract/return), take out (extract/invite out).

questions.stem: The old man struggled to make ______ what the foreign visitor was saying.
questions.explanation: B is correct. MAKE OUT = (1) to understand or decipher; (2) to claim or pretend; (3) to write a cheque. In this context: 'couldn't make out what was being said' = couldn't understand. 'Make' phrasal verbs: make up (invent/reconcile), make out (understand/pretend), make off (flee), make over (transform), make do with (manage with), make for (head towards).

questions.stem: She decided to set ______ early to avoid the morning traffic.
questions.explanation: B is correct. SET OUT = to begin a journey or start working towards a goal. 'Set off' also means to begin a journey, but the question expects 'set out'. Note: in many exams, 'set out' implies a planned journey with a clear destination. 'Set' phrasal verbs: set up (establish), set out (begin journey/state), set aside (reserve), set back (delay), set off (trigger/begin journey).

questions.stem: The volunteer programme was set ______ to help underprivileged children.
questions.explanation: C is correct. SET UP = to establish, create, or organise something (a company, programme, meeting). 'The programme was set up' = the programme was established/created. Note the contrast: 'set out' = begin journey; 'set up' = establish. These two are easily confused in exams.

questions.stem: The loud noise broke ______ their conversation.
questions.explanation: A is correct. BREAK UP = (1) to end a relationship or group; (2) to disrupt/interrupt. 'Broke up their conversation' = disrupted and ended their conversation. 'Break' phrasal verbs: break up (end/disrupt), break down (fail/cry), break out (escape/begin), break in (interrupt/enter by force), break off (stop abruptly), break through (overcome).

questions.stem: Which phrasal verb means 'to postpone or delay something'?
questions.explanation: B is correct. PUT OFF = to postpone or delay. Also means: to discourage or cause someone to lose interest ('The bad smell put her off her food'). Turn down = reject/reduce volume. Get over = recover. Run out = use up. Synonyms of 'put off' (postpone): defer, delay, reschedule, shelve.

questions.stem: After months of effort, they finally came ______ a solution to the problem.
questions.explanation: B is correct. COME UP WITH = to produce, think of, or create something (a plan, idea, solution) through effort. 'They came up with a solution' = they thought of/produced a solution. Compare: come across (find unexpectedly), come up with (produce through thought), come around (recover/agree), come down to (be fundamentally about).

questions.stem: The old factory was eventually torn ______ to make way for a new mall.
questions.explanation: B is correct. TEAR DOWN = to demolish or destroy a building or structure. 'The factory was torn down' = the factory was demolished. Tear up = rip into small pieces (letters/paper). Tear apart = rip into pieces or cause emotional distress. This is an important phrasal verb in passages about urban development.
